blocks.c: Book cover of Mick Herron's 'Joe Country'

blocks.x: Widely regarded by the fans of the Slough House series as its emotional high, Joe Country brings several long-running plot threads to a close and delivers at least one genuinely heartbreaking farewell to a beloved character (but no spoilers here). Set partly in the Welsh countryside, a jarring change of scenery from Herron's typical London-bound universe, it follows Louisa Guy to Pembrokeshire as she searches for Lucas, the teenage son of her late partner Min Harper, who has gone missing after seeing something he was never supposed to see. Frank Harkness, a renegade ex-CIA operative, looms over the whole novel like a storm that keeps on brewing.

Joe Country is essential because it is the book that proves Herron is not just an extraordinarily witty and clever writer but has the chops to write something genuinely moving. The comedy is still present and sharp, but here it exists in direct tension with loss in a way the series hadn't previously attempted. Crime Fiction Lover called it "a triumph" and "the series highlight" at the time of publication. For readers who have followed the slow horses from the beginning, this novel earns every feeling it reaches for. The upcoming Season 6 partly adapts Joe Country, and we're not sure if we're fully saying goodbye or another hello to Rosalind Eleazar as the brilliant Louisa Guy.

blocks.c: Book cover of Mick Herron's 'Dead Lions'

blocks.x: Dead Lions is the novel that put Herron on the map; it won the Crime Writers' Association Gold Dagger Award, the most prestigious prize in British crime fiction. This is the novel that most clearly announces what the Slough House series is capable of, though not all critics would agree it's the best Herron has to give—and yet, it's so brilliant, you can only imagine what the rest have to offer. Dead Lions is essential because it reveals Jackson Lamb's past a little more, involving the apparent murder of a former Cold War sleeper agent and the reactivation of old Soviet networks that nobody believed were still active. This leans into classic le Carré territory but is handled with Herron's characteristically sardonic twist. Lamb is given significantly more room to operate here than in the debut.

What Dead Lions gets exactly right is the balance between genuine spy thriller mechanics and dark comic character work; this is the balance that the rest of the series would later be built on, and Herron achieves it here with particular elegance. The Cold War material feels neither nostalgic nor exhausted, rather bringing the shabbiness of modern-day Slough House into a sharp focus. Dead Lions is also just one of the most entertaining thrillers of its decade, an essential entry point for anyone arriving from the TV show and wondering where to begin with the books. With Season 2 of Slow Horses having been done with great precision, Dead Lions (Season 2's source material) will be an even more impressive feat to enjoy after the show.

blocks.c: A man walking in a neon rain-soaked street on the cover of Clown Town

blocks.x: The ninth and most recent novel, Clown Town, is a true game-changer in the Slough House series. This one resolves two of the series' longest-running power struggles: the tension between Peter Judd and Diana Taverner and the uneasy standoff between Taverner and Lamb. Simultaneously, it upends the status quo in ways that leave Slough House's future genuinely uncertain for the first time. River Cartwright, recovering from a case of poisoning, is drawn into a mystery surrounding a missing book from his grandfather David's library. Meanwhile, Taverner, threatened by figures connected to a covert operation from the height of the Troubles, turns blackmail into opportunity, as she always does.

The Spectator Australia named Clown Town one of its books of the year, calling it "a magisterially accomplished novel" with "a plot of shining, machine-like efficiency." What makes Clown Town essential is not just its quality but its finality; it closes doors that have been open since book one, takes some meaningful casualties, and arrives at an ending that is the very definition of the word "cliffhanger." If you have read the Slough House series from the start, Clown Town is the payoff; if you haven't, well, this is the most compelling argument for starting the series immediately.

blocks.c: Book cover of Mick Herron's 'Slough House'

blocks.x: The seventh novel is where Herron's ambitions expand from spy thriller to something closer to a state-of-the-nation novel: a panoramic, almost Dickensian portrait of Britain at its most paranoid and compromised. Brexit has pushed the slow horses further into the cold, Slough House has been erased from official records, and members of the team are dying at an unsettling clip. The satire extends far beyond intelligence services this time, reaching into media manipulation, global finance, and the privatization of state power, a territory Herron navigates with the confidence of a writer who has been building toward exactly this for a decade.

Universally, the unnerving realism of Slough House (the novel) has been considered as Herron gone spooky, with the satire getting even more biting and the comedy developing harder edges. Slough House is essential because it is the novel that makes the fullest case for what the series actually is: a genuinely serious piece of contemporary fiction that just so happens to operate through the conventions of the spy thriller. This one converted casual fans into devotees, and it's the one that most convincingly demands to be taken seriously on its own terms. Season 6 partly adapts Slough House, meaning that the stakes are growing higher and more real within the Slow Horses TV universe.

blocks.c: A man standing with his hands tied with a rope in the forefront on the cover for Slow Horses

blocks.x: The one novel that started everything and is still the most essential of all is the first book, Slow Horses, because without it, none of the rest exists. Like in the series, River Cartwright lands at Slough House in disgrace after a training exercise goes catastrophically wrong in a very public way. Then a young man is kidnapped and threatened with beheading by a group claiming to be terrorists, and the slow horses begin noticing inconsistencies that lead them into a conspiracy with roots deep inside MI5 itself. The plot is gripping, and the atmosphere, with its unglamorous, rain-soaked, bureaucratic exhaustion, is immediately distinctive from other similar novels.

What makes Slow Horses essential rather than merely good is Jackson Lamb, and this applies to both the novels and the TV show. He arrives fully formed as one of the great characters in modern crime fiction: self-sufficient, brilliant, and oddly principled in ways that take an entire series to fully understand. Every subsequent book depends on the reader's relationship with Lamb, which is established here; it's hard to read the books without imagining Gary Oldman, who portrays Lamb in the Apple TV adaptation, and he seems to perfectly embody the spy's description from the books. The show is excellent, of course, sometimes so much that it's hard to imagine what the novels might represent. And yet, even here, we do get to say—the books are better, just because they establish a world so detailed and incredible that you will be drawn in to the very end.
Adam Randall, James Hawes, Jeremy Lovering, Saul Metzstein
Douglas Urbanski, Emile Sherman, Gail Mutrux, Graham Yost, Hakan Kousetta, Iain Canning, James Hawes, Jamie Laurenson, Jane Robertson, Julian Stevens, Will Smith

Chigurh does not negotiate, gloat or explain. He arrives, he asks one question, and the
answer was decided long before you opened your mouth.

You trust yourself to handle things. He is the one problem in the world that has no
interest in how capable you are.

No Country for Old Men rewrote the screen villain by removing the thing audiences
quietly rely on: the sense that talking might work.

Call it. He will wait.

'Joe Country' (2019)

Image via John Murray

Widely regarded by the fans of the Slough House series as its emotional high, Joe Country brings several long-running plot threads to a close and delivers at least one genuinely heartbreaking farewell to a beloved character (but no spoilers here). Set partly in the Welsh countryside, a jarring change of scenery from Herron's typical London-bound universe, it follows Louisa Guy to Pembrokeshire as she searches for Lucas, the teenage son of her late partner Min Harper, who has gone missing after seeing something he was never supposed to see. Frank Harkness, a renegade ex-CIA operative, looms over the whole novel like a storm that keeps on brewing.

Joe Country is essential because it is the book that proves Herron is not just an extraordinarily witty and clever writer but has the chops to write something genuinely moving. The comedy is still present and sharp, but here it exists in direct tension with loss in a way the series hadn't previously attempted. Crime Fiction Lover called it "a triumph" and "the series highlight" at the time of publication. For readers who have followed the slow horses from the beginning, this novel earns every feeling it reaches for. The upcoming Season 6 partly adapts Joe Country, and we're not sure if we're fully saying goodbye or another hello to Rosalind Eleazar as the brilliant Louisa Guy.

'Dead Lions' (2013)

Image via John Murray

Dead Lions is the novel that put Herron on the map; it won the Crime Writers' Association Gold Dagger Award, the most prestigious prize in British crime fiction. This is the novel that most clearly announces what the Slough House series is capable of, though not all critics would agree it's the best Herron has to give—and yet, it's so brilliant, you can only imagine what the rest have to offer. Dead Lions is essential because it reveals Jackson Lamb's past a little more, involving the apparent murder of a former Cold War sleeper agent and the reactivation of old Soviet networks that nobody believed were still active. This leans into classic le Carré territory but is handled with Herron's characteristically sardonic twist. Lamb is given significantly more room to operate here than in the debut.

What Dead Lions gets exactly right is the balance between genuine spy thriller mechanics and dark comic character work; this is the balance that the rest of the series would later be built on, and Herron achieves it here with particular elegance. The Cold War material feels neither nostalgic nor exhausted, rather bringing the shabbiness of modern-day Slough House into a sharp focus. Dead Lions is also just one of the most entertaining thrillers of its decade, an essential entry point for anyone arriving from the TV show and wondering where to begin with the books. With Season 2 of Slow Horses having been done with great precision, Dead Lions (Season 2's source material) will be an even more impressive feat to enjoy after the show.

'Clown Town' (2025)

Image via Hachette UK

The ninth and most recent novel, Clown Town, is a true game-changer in the Slough House series. This one resolves two of the series' longest-running power struggles: the tension between Peter Judd and Diana Taverner and the uneasy standoff between Taverner and Lamb. Simultaneously, it upends the status quo in ways that leave Slough House's future genuinely uncertain for the first time. River Cartwright, recovering from a case of poisoning, is drawn into a mystery surrounding a missing book from his grandfather David's library. Meanwhile, Taverner, threatened by figures connected to a covert operation from the height of the Troubles, turns blackmail into opportunity, as she always does.

The Spectator Australia named Clown Town one of its books of the year, calling it "a magisterially accomplished novel" with "a plot of shining, machine-like efficiency." What makes Clown Town essential is not just its quality but its finality; it closes doors that have been open since book one, takes some meaningful casualties, and arrives at an ending that is the very definition of the word "cliffhanger." If you have read the Slough House series from the start, Clown Town is the payoff; if you haven't, well, this is the most compelling argument for starting the series immediately.

'Slough House' (2021)

Image via Soho Crime

The seventh novel is where Herron's ambitions expand from spy thriller to something closer to a state-of-the-nation novel: a panoramic, almost Dickensian portrait of Britain at its most paranoid and compromised. Brexit has pushed the slow horses further into the cold, Slough House has been erased from official records, and members of the team are dying at an unsettling clip. The satire extends far beyond intelligence services this time, reaching into media manipulation, global finance, and the privatization of state power, a territory Herron navigates with the confidence of a writer who has been building toward exactly this for a decade.

Universally, the unnerving realism of Slough House (the novel) has been considered as Herron gone spooky, with the satire getting even more biting and the comedy developing harder edges. Slough House is essential because it is the novel that makes the fullest case for what the series actually is: a genuinely serious piece of contemporary fiction that just so happens to operate through the conventions of the spy thriller. This one converted casual fans into devotees, and it's the one that most convincingly demands to be taken seriously on its own terms. Season 6 partly adapts Slough House, meaning that the stakes are growing higher and more real within the Slow Horses TV universe.

'Slow Horses' (2010)

Image via Soho Constable

The one novel that started everything and is still the most essential of all is the first book, Slow Horses, because without it, none of the rest exists. Like in the series, River Cartwright lands at Slough House in disgrace after a training exercise goes catastrophically wrong in a very public way. Then a young man is kidnapped and threatened with beheading by a group claiming to be terrorists, and the slow horses begin noticing inconsistencies that lead them into a conspiracy with roots deep inside MI5 itself. The plot is gripping, and the atmosphere, with its unglamorous, rain-soaked, bureaucratic exhaustion, is immediately distinctive from other similar novels.

What makes Slow Horses essential rather than merely good is Jackson Lamb, and this applies to both the novels and the TV show. He arrives fully formed as one of the great characters in modern crime fiction: self-sufficient, brilliant, and oddly principled in ways that take an entire series to fully understand. Every subsequent book depends on the reader's relationship with Lamb, which is established here; it's hard to read the books without imagining Gary Oldman, who portrays Lamb in the Apple TV adaptation, and he seems to perfectly embody the spy's description from the books. The show is excellent, of course, sometimes so much that it's hard to imagine what the novels might represent. And yet, even here, we do get to say—the books are better, just because they establish a world so detailed and incredible that you will be drawn in to the very end.
